heading_path.h3: Worked example 12.14: Comparing methods of calculating area of a rectangle

records.raw_html:
Worked example 12.14: Comparing methods of calculating area of a rectangle

Find the area of the rectangle provided by counting squares. Each square on the grid represents a square of 1 km by 1 km. Then work out a formula for calculating the area of a rectangle, and check the answer you get by comparing it to your first answer.

  1. Step 1: Remember that area is the amount of flat space taken up by a shape. Count the number of squares on the grid that are covered by the rectangle.

    The rectangle consists of 9 columns of smaller squares. Each column has 4 smaller squares. So there are 9 4 = 36 squares inside the rectangle.

    Area of rectangle = 36 km

  2. Step 2: Use your calculation above to work out a formula to calculate the area of a rectangle.

    You can see that 9 km is the length of the rectangle, and 4 km is the breadth. To get the area, you multiplied 9 by 4, so what you did was multiply the length by the breadth. Then you wrote in the square units, which this time is km.

    So the formula for the area of a rectangle is length breadth.

  3. Step 3: Use the formula to calculate the area.

  4. Step 4: Compare this answer with your first answer.

    Both methods give the same answer: A = 36 km.
records.prompt_text: Find the area of the rectangle provided by counting squares. Each square on the grid represents a square of 1 km by 1 km. Then work out a formula for calculating the area of a rectangle, and check the answer you get by comparing it to your first answer.
records.answer_text:
Step 1: Remember that area is the amount of flat space taken up by a shape. Count the number of squares on the grid that are covered by the rectangle.

The rectangle consists of 9 columns of smaller squares. Each column has 4 smaller squares. So there are 9 $\times$ 4 = 36 squares inside the rectangle.

Area of rectangle = 36 km$^{2}$

Step 2: Use your calculation above to work out a formula to calculate the area of a rectangle.

You can see that 9 km is the length of the rectangle, and 4 km is the breadth. To get the area, you multiplied 9 by 4, so what you did was multiply the length by the breadth. Then you wrote in the square units, which this time is km$^{2}$.

So the formula for the area of a rectangle is length $\times$ breadth.

Step 3: Use the formula to calculate the area.

$$
\begin{array}{ll}
\text{Area of rectangle} &{= \text{length} \times \text{breadth}}\\
&{= l \times b} \\
&{= \text{9 km} \times \text{4 km}} \\
&{= \text{36}\ {\text{km}^{2}}}
\end{array}
$$

Step 4: Compare this answer with your first answer.

Both methods give the same answer: A = 36 km$^{2}$.

records.raw_html:
Worked example 12.15: Comparing methods of calculating area of a square

Find the area of the square provided by counting squares. Each square on the grid represents a square of 1 cm by 1 cm. Then work out a formula for calculating the area of a square, and check the answer you get by comparing it to your first answer.

  1. Step 1: Count the number of squares on the grid that are covered by the square.

    The square consists of 9 rows of squares and 9 columns of squares. So there are 9 9 = 81 squares inside the square.

    Area of square = 81 cm

  2. Step 2: Use your calculation to work out a formula to calculate the area of a square.

    In a square, all four sides are the same length. To get the area, you multiplied 9 by 9, so what you did was multiply the length by the length (or we can say the side by the side). So the area is just the product of the two (equal) sides. Then you wrote in the square units, which this time is cm.

    So the formula for the area of a square is side side.

  3. Step 3: Use the formula to calculate the area.

  4. Step 4: Compare this answer with your first answer.

    Both methods give the same answer: A = 81 cm.

heading_path.h3: Formulae for the area of a two-dimensional shape

records.raw_html:
It will help you if you memorise the formulae for area, so that you can use them easily when you need to. Understanding where the formulae come from will help you to memorise them.

  • Rectangle: Area of a rectangle = length breadth.

  • Square: Area of a square

  • Triangle: Area of a triangle .

    The base (b) and the height (h) of a triangle are labelled in the diagram above. It is very important with a triangle that the base and the height are perpendicular to each other, or you will not get the correct answer.

  • Parallelogram: Area of a parallelogram .

    It is also important that the base (b) and the height (h) of a rectangle are perpendicular to each other.

  • Trapezium: Area of a trapezium .

    The two parallel sides of the trapezium (a and b) must be perpendicular to the height (h) of the trapezium.

  • Circle: Area of a circle .

    Remember that r is the radius of the circle.
records.content_text:
It will help you if you memorise the formulae for area, so that you can use them easily when you need to. Understanding where the formulae come from will help you to memorise them.

- **Rectangle:** Area of a rectangle = length $\times$ breadth.
- **Square:** Area of a square $= s \times s = s^{2}$
- **Triangle:** Area of a triangle $= \frac{b \times h}{2}$.
- **Parallelogram:** Area of a parallelogram $= b \times h$.
- **Trapezium:** Area of a trapezium $= \frac{h}{2}\left( a + b \right)$.
- **Circle:** Area of a circle $= \pi \times r^{2}$.

With a triangle, the base ($b$) and the height ($h$) must be perpendicular to each other, or you will not get the correct answer.
